solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Rocky 6 — in a rut, Hugh Jackman? (10)

indicators.note: rocky = unsteady, so the letters wobble into a new order

annotation.surface: A fan laments a sixth Rocky film that has left its star stuck in a rut.
annotation.walkthrough: Rocky looks like the Stallone franchise, with 6 as a sequel number; it is the anagram signal, and 6 is a cross-reference to ALAS. The question mark flags a definition by example: Jackman is one Australian.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Wolverine star was born in Sydney, and the question mark admits he is only one instance.

clue.text: Two lines required to capture this / fish (5)

definitions.text: Two lines required to capture this

blocks.clueFragment: Two lines required to capture this
blocks.note: a geometric figure made where two lines meet; 'capture' = draw
a verb: to try to catch fish with rod and line

annotation.surface: An angler explains that landing this catch takes two fishing lines.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half pretends to be about fishing lines; they are geometric lines, and 'capture' means to draw or represent.
annotation.definitionFit: An angle is the figure formed where two lines meet; to angle is to fish with a line.

clue.text: Petition to eat BLT with filling that’s extended [and] purified (9)

definitions.note: Sublimate as an adjective (chemistry) means purified by sublimation.

indicators.note: what eats something takes it inside, so SUE goes around the rest

blocks.note: to sue = to petition, split around the rest
BLT's filling letter is L, written out as its NATO call-sign Lima

annotation.surface: Someone lodges a formal request to be allowed to eat a bacon, lettuce and tomato sandwich.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'filling' is not bacon or lettuce but the middle letter of the abbreviation, and 'extended' means spelling that letter out the way radio operators do. The chemistry sense of the definition is the unfamiliar part.
annotation.definitionFit: In chemistry, to sublimate a substance is to purify it by turning solid to vapour and back, so sublimated means purified; the past participle is sublimate in older use.

clue.text: Act surprised as Obi-Wan, Rey and ultimately Luke Skywalker are cast (5,2,7)

indicators.note: ultimately = in the end, so take the final letters
to cast is to throw, so the letters are thrown into a new order

annotation.surface: A fan is startled by the casting of a Star Wars film with Obi-Wan, Rey and Luke Skywalker.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cast' reads as film casting, which fits the Star Wars names perfectly; it is the anagram signal. 'Ultimately' applies to each of the last three words.
annotation.definitionFit: Raising an eyebrow is the classic gesture of mild surprise, so doing it is acting surprised.

clue.text: They show unqualified person recently breaking records (1-6)

indicators.note: what breaks into something sits inside it

blocks.note: LPs = long-playing records, split around the rest

annotation.surface: A newcomer with no qualifications has lately been setting records.
annotation.walkthrough: L-plates are the red L signs a British learner driver must display, so they show the driver has not yet passed the test.
annotation.definitionFit: L-plates tell other road users that the driver is a learner, an unqualified person.

clue.text: Two articles about permitted jumper? (7)

indicators.note: about = around, so the articles go around LET

blocks.note: the definite article, split around LET

annotation.surface: Some writing about a sweater that is allowed, perhaps in a dress code.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' looks like a British word for a sweater; the question mark says it is a person who jumps, one kind of athlete.
annotation.definitionFit: A high jumper or long jumper is an athlete, so a jumper is an example of one.

clue.text: Festivals starting late, unfortunately (4)

indicators.note: a word that starts late has lost its first letter

blocks.note: GALAS without its first letter G

annotation.surface: Regretfully, the festivals got off to a late start.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Starting late' reads as a delay to the festivals; it means the word GALAS begins one letter later.
annotation.definitionFit: Alas is an exclamation of regret, used just like 'unfortunately'.

clue.text: Legitimate Literature 101 dons (5)

indicators.note: to don is to put on, so LIT wears CI

annotation.surface: An introductory literature course is a real, accredited class.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Literature 101' looks like an American entry-level course code; the number is Roman CI, and 'dons' may suggest university teachers but is the verb 'puts on'.
annotation.definitionFit: Licit means lawful, the same as legitimate.

clue.text: Dripping [is] like some fat (9)

blocks.note: fat whose carbon chains hold all the hydrogen they can, as on food labels

annotation.surface: Dripping, the cooking fat from roast meat, counts as a kind of fat.
annotation.walkthrough: Dripping is British for fat collected from roasting meat, which makes the surface look like a statement about cooking fat; here it means soaking wet.
annotation.definitionFit: Something saturated is soaked, dripping wet; saturated fat is a type of dietary fat.

clue.text: Abrupt Times editor: undo changes [in] our masthead text! (4,2,3,5)

indicators.note: abrupt = cut short, so TIMES loses its last letter
the letters change their order

annotation.surface: A brusque Times editor orders changes to be undone in the paper's own masthead.
annotation.walkthrough: The Times masthead carries the royal coat of arms, whose motto is Dieu et mon droit (God and my right). 'Undo' is fodder, not an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: The motto on the royal arms at the top of The Times front page is Dieu et mon droit, literally text on its masthead.

clue.text: Biblical messenger[’s] talk that is splitting sides (7)

indicators.note: IE splits the sides apart by going between them

blocks.note: right and left, split around IE

annotation.surface: An angel's announcement is so funny that it has listeners splitting their sides.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Splitting sides' suggests laughter; it means IE goes between R and L, the two sides.
annotation.definitionFit: Gabriel is the archangel who brings God's messages in the Bible, notably the Annunciation.

clue.text: Do musical score? (7)

blocks.note: to score = to cut a line into

annotation.surface: A question: can you perform the score of a musical?
annotation.walkthrough: 'Do' reads as a verb and 'score' as music, both from the stage; a do is a hairdo, and score means cut.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal British sense: a do is a hairdo, the style a barber or stylist leaves you with.

clue.text: Most intense part [of] impressive dish that’s unfinished (9)

indicators.note: the word is left without its last letter

annotation.surface: The best bit of a grand meal comes from a course that nobody finished.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Most intense part' sounds like a food critic's praise; it is the definition. EPICENTRE is spelt the British way.
annotation.definitionFit: The epicentre of something is its focal point, where it is most intense, like an earthquake's.

clue.text: Like croissants without ends, say (5)

indicators.note: the word loses its first and last letters

blocks.note: BUTTERY without its ends B and Y

annotation.surface: Something is like croissants that have had their tips nibbled off, for instance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example' tacked on the end; it is the definition, a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: both mean to put words into speech.

clue.text: Open banana avoided by worker, perhaps (5)

indicators.note: the banana word avoids ANT, so those letters are dropped from it

blocks.note: a plantain is a cooking banana
the worker ant, one example of a worker; removed from PLANTAIN

annotation.surface: A peeled banana is left alone by a worker, maybe on an insect trail.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Open banana' reads as a peeled fruit, but 'Open' is the definition on its own. Taking ANT from PLANTAIN leaves PLAIN.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain as in open and obvious, or an open stretch of flat land.

clue.text: Useful feature for table fork, with peace shattered (5,4)

indicators.note: shattered things are broken up, so the letters break and re-form

annotation.surface: A fork is handy at the dinner table, though peace is broken over the meal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Table' suggests dining next to 'fork'; it is a card table, where a poker face hides your hand.
annotation.definitionFit: A poker face gives nothing away, which is useful at a card table.

clue.text: Confectionery with marijuana? It’s a bit of a racket (5,4)

definitions.text: It’s a bit of a racket

annotation.surface: Selling cannabis sweets is a dodgy business, a bit of a racket.
annotation.walkthrough: A racket here is a tennis racket, not a scam; the sweet spot is the area of the strings that hits the ball best.
annotation.definitionFit: The sweet spot is the part of a racket that gives the best shot, so it is literally a bit of a racket.

clue.text: Aha! House of Commons censure over game (9)

indicators.note: in a down clue, over turns the letters upside down, reading them backwards

blocks.note: 'I see!' is an exclamation of realisation, like 'Aha!'
HC is the abbreviation for House of Commons

annotation.surface: An MP is caught out and the House of Commons rebukes him over some political game.
annotation.walkthrough: All three pieces are strung together as I SEE, HC, RAP and then the whole chain is read backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Parcheesi is a board game, an American version of the Indian game pachisi.

clue.text: Glance over young professional[’s] football skills (5-4)

indicators.note: over = turned over, so PEEK is reversed

annotation.surface: A scout looks over a young player's football skills.
annotation.walkthrough: Keepy-uppy is the British name for keeping a football in the air with feet, knees and head, a show of ball skills.
annotation.definitionFit: Keepy-uppy is the trick of juggling a football without letting it touch the ground.

clue.text: Channel covering mixed martial arts after 12 (3-4)

indicators.note: in a down clue, the piece that covers another sits on top of it

blocks.note: a pipe is a channel for fluid

annotation.surface: A TV channel is showing cage fighting after midday.
annotation.walkthrough: Channel reads as a TV station, pairing with the sport; it is a pipe. Pip emma is old British signallers' talk for p.m., the letters P and M in their phonetic alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: Pip emma means p.m., the hours after 12 noon.

clue.text: Who’s looking at this African nation, ignoring one more recently created? (7)

indicators.note: the word ignores the one, leaving it out

blocks.note: the person reading the clue is you

annotation.surface: A question about who is studying a certain African country, passing over a newer state.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Who's looking at this' addresses the solver directly: the answer is YOU. Niger is the West African country.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain comparative synonym: of lesser age means brought into being at a later date.

clue.text: Did row ultimately undo American revolutionary? (5)

indicators.note: ultimately = finally, so take the last letter

annotation.surface: A question: did a quarrel in the end bring down an American rebel?
annotation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests an argument; it is rowing a boat, and 'Did row' is past tense, matching OARED.
annotation.definitionFit: To oar is to row, so oared means rowed.

clue.text: Shape [of] mug that H&M cut apart (5)

indicators.note: H and M cut into the word at two separate places

blocks.note: H goes after R, M after O

annotation.surface: A mug design that a high-street clothes chain has sliced up.
annotation.walkthrough: H&M is the clothing chain, but here it is just the letters H and M, which go into ROB separately rather than together.
annotation.definitionFit: A rhomb, or rhombus, is a four-sided shape with equal sides.

clue.text: Someone paid by the state to stock books, available as needed (2,3)

indicators.note: the pensioner stocks the books, holding them inside

blocks.note: OAP = old-age pensioner, paid a state pension; split around NT
NT = New Testament, a set of books

annotation.surface: A public employee has to keep the library shelves stocked with books for readers who need them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Someone paid by the state' suggests a civil servant; it is a British old-age pensioner, OAP.
annotation.definitionFit: Something on tap is ready whenever you want it, like beer from a tap.

clue.text: Inferior work following exclusive about a French duke (9)

definitions.note: Pound shop is a noun used attributively (pound-shop goods) to mean cheap or inferior.

indicators.note: work comes after the rest
about = surrounding, so the exclusive word is placed around the French article and duke

blocks.note: posh = upmarket, exclusive; split around UND

annotation.surface: A shoddy piece of work comes after an exclusive story about a French aristocrat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Inferior work' looks like the definition; only 'Inferior' is, and work is OP. A pound shop is a British store where everything costs one pound.
annotation.definitionFit: A pound shop sells cheap goods, so 'pound-shop' describes anything cheap and inferior.

clue.text: Way to conceal Conservative plot (5)

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hide it away, so the way keeps the Conservative out of sight inside itself

blocks.note: a path = a way; split around C

annotation.surface: A way for the Tories to hide their scheming.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plot' sounds like a conspiracy beside the Conservatives; it is a plot of land.
annotation.definitionFit: A patch is a small plot of ground, like a vegetable patch.

clue.text: Sweetheart for many encapsulates poetry? (3,4)

indicators.note: the phrase holds the answer inside it

annotation.surface: A beloved of many people sums up all that poetry is.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks poetry as one example of an art form.
annotation.definitionFit: Poetry is one art form among others such as music and painting.

clue.text: Most tacky introduction for Iggy and Stooges briefly broadcast (7)

indicators.note: the introduction of a word is its first letter
cut short by its last letter
broadcast = scattered widely, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: Stooges without its last letter S

annotation.surface: The cheesiest broadcast of the night introduces Iggy Pop and his punk band the Stooges.
annotation.walkthrough: Iggy and the Stooges were a real US punk band, so 'broadcast' seems to mean airplay; it signals an anagram. Tacky here means sticky.
annotation.definitionFit: Tacky can mean sticky, so the most tacky thing is the gooiest.

clue.text: Notice essay has page replacing it (4)

indicators.note: to replace something is to take its place, so the page letter stands where 'it' stood in the essay

blocks.note: it = SA, sex appeal; removed from ESSAY
p = page; put where SA was

annotation.surface: A teacher notices that a student's essay has an extra page slipped in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'It' is crossword shorthand for sex appeal, SA. Swapping those two letters of ESSAY for P gives ESPY.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain, slightly literary verb synonym: both mean to catch sight of something.

clue.text: Churchgoers welcoming corrupt female swimmer (10)

indicators.note: the parish welcomes ROT F inside

blocks.note: a parish = the congregation of a church; split around ROTF

annotation.surface: A congregation takes in a woman of dubious morals who is keen on swimming.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' seems to belong to the female in the surface; it is the definition, a fish.
annotation.definitionFit: The parrotfish is a brightly coloured reef fish, so it is a swimmer.
